What test did the Supreme Court adopt in Patel v Mirza for whether illegality bars a claim, and what did it replace?

key_points: Rejected the reliance test from Tinsley v Milligan [1994] 1 AC 340
Lord Toulson's trio of considerations: underlying purpose of the prohibition, other relevant public policies, proportionality of denying the claim
Claimant in Patel recovered the money paid (restitution) despite the illegal insider-dealing agreement

prompt: State the test for dishonesty set out in Ivey v Genting Casinos and explain its status in criminal law.

key_points: Stage 1: ascertain subjectively the actual state of the individual's knowledge or belief as to the facts
Stage 2: was the conduct dishonest by the (objective) standards of ordinary decent people; no requirement that the defendant appreciated it was dishonest
Second limb of R v Ghosh disapproved (obiter in a civil case)
Confirmed as binding in criminal law by the Court of Appeal in R v Barton and Booth [2020] EWCA Crim 575

prompt: What did the Supreme Court decide in Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire Police about the 'Caparo test'?

key_points: Caparo does not establish a universal tripartite test for every case
In established categories apply existing law; in novel cases develop the law incrementally by analogy
Police not generally immune; liable for positive acts causing foreseeable physical injury (claimant succeeded)
Distinction between acts and omissions remains

prompt: What did the Supreme Court decide in Uber BV v Aslam and what interpretive approach did it take?

key_points: Drivers were 'workers' under s 230(3)(b) Employment Rights Act 1996
Purposive approach to the statute; written terms not the starting point (Autoclenz)
Factors of control: Uber fixed fares, contract terms, ratings/deactivation, restricted communication
Working time included periods logged into the app in the territory and ready to accept trips

prompt: Explain the test for a penalty clause after Cavendish Square Holding BV v Makdessi.

key_points: Test: whether the clause is a secondary obligation imposing a detriment out of all proportion to any legitimate interest of the innocent party in performance
Rejected the 'genuine pre-estimate of loss' test as decisive (Dunlop)
Primary obligations are not subject to the penalty rule
Decided with ParkingEye Ltd v Beavis; both clauses upheld

prompt: What did Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board decide about a doctor's duty to disclose risks?

key_points: Duty to take reasonable care to ensure the patient is aware of any material risks and reasonable alternatives
Materiality: whether a reasonable person in the patient's position would attach significance, or the doctor knows/should know this patient would
Bolam / Sidaway (majority approach) no longer applies to disclosure
Limited therapeutic exception

prompt: Are no-oral-modification clauses effective in English law? Explain with reference to the leading case.

key_points: Yes: Rock Advertising v MWB [2018] UKSC 24 - NOM clauses give effect to party autonomy and are legally effective
Oral variation ineffective unless it complies with the formalities
Estoppel may provide a safeguard, but requires more than the informal promise itself
Consideration point (Williams v Roffey / Foakes v Beer) left open

prompt: What is the Quincecare duty and how did Philipp v Barclays Bank affect it?

key_points: Quincecare duty: bank should not execute an agent's instruction where it has reasonable grounds to believe it is an attempt to misappropriate the customer's funds
Philipp: duty is an application of the bank's duty to act on instructions with reasonable care, and does not arise where the customer personally authorises the payment (APP fraud victim)
Mrs Philipp's claim on that basis failed
Possible separate claim regarding recovery of funds after notification left for trial

prompt: After Stack v Dowden and Jones v Kernott, how is beneficial ownership of a jointly-registered family home determined?

key_points: Starting point: equity follows the law - joint beneficial tenancy
Burden on the party seeking to show different shares
Whole course of dealing in relation to the property is considered to infer (or, if necessary, impute) common intention as to shares
Jones v Kernott [2011] UKSC 53: intentions may change over time; court may impute fair shares if intention cannot be inferred

prompt: What did the Supreme Court decide in Tindall v Chief Constable of Thames Valley Police?

key_points: Police owed no duty of care to the deceased driver
Police had not made matters worse: they did not create the danger or put off others from helping
Failure to confer a benefit (an omission) does not generally found a duty; no assumption of responsibility
Appeal dismissed

prompt: A defendant is charged with theft. Explain how the jury should apply the Ghosh test to decide whether he was dishonest.

key_points: Ghosh second (subjective) limb no longer good law
Ivey v Genting [2017] UKSC 67 test applies; confirmed in criminal law by R v Barton and Booth [2020] EWCA Crim 575

prompt: Applying Tinsley v Milligan, can a claimant who transferred property to conceal it from creditors recover it, given that she does not need to rely on her illegal purpose?

key_points: Reliance test in Tinsley v Milligan replaced by Patel v Mirza [2016] UKSC 42
Apply trio of considerations / range of factors

prompt: Under the principle in R v Powell and Chan Wing-Siu, is it enough for a secondary party to have foreseen that the principal might commit murder?

key_points: R v Jogee [2016] UKSC 8 held that the law took a wrong turn; foresight is evidence of intent, not sufficient in itself
Secondary party must intend to assist or encourage the principal's crime, with knowledge of essential matters

prompt: My barrister ran my trial negligently. I understand barristers have immunity from suit for advocacy under Rondel v Worsley. Is that right?

key_points: Advocates' immunity abolished by Arthur JS Hall & Co v Simons [2002] 1 AC 615
Collateral attack on a criminal conviction may still be an abuse of process

prompt: Apply the two-stage test from Anns v Merton London Borough Council to decide whether a local authority owes a duty of care to a homeowner for pure economic loss caused by a defective foundation inspection.

key_points: Anns overruled by Murphy v Brentwood DC [1991] 1 AC 398
Pure economic loss for defective buildings generally irrecoverable in tort against the council
Caparo / Robinson incremental approach

prompt: A surgeon did not mention a 1% risk of serious harm. Under the Bolam test, if a responsible body of surgeons would not have mentioned it, is the surgeon liable?

key_points: For risk disclosure Bolam replaced by Montgomery [2015] UKSC 11 materiality test
Bolam still governs diagnosis and treatment

prompt: Under the Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre test, a liquidated damages clause is a penalty unless it is a genuine pre-estimate of loss. Apply that test to a clause requiring a £50,000 payment for late completion.

prompt: Explain how Caldwell recklessness applies to a charge of criminal damage.

key_points: Caldwell overruled by R v G [2003] UKHL 50
Subjective test: defendant aware of a risk and unreasonable to take it

key_points: Divorce, Dissolution and Separation Act 2020 (in force 6 April 2022) introduced no-fault divorce
Statement of irretrievable breakdown is conclusive; defending on the facts is no longer possible (only jurisdiction / validity etc.)

prompt: Can a claimant recover punitive damages for a deliberate breach of contract in England?

key_points: Punitive/exemplary damages not available for breach of contract (Addis v Gramophone Co [1909] AC 488)
Account of profits exceptionally: Attorney General v Blake [2001] 1 AC 268
Negotiating damages: Morris-Garner v One Step [2018] UKSC 20

prompt: When police in England arrest a suspect, must they read him his Miranda rights? What happens if they don't?

key_points: Miranda is US law; not applicable
Caution under PACE 1984 Code C (right to silence, adverse inferences under s 34 CJPOA 1994)
Breach may lead to exclusion under s 76/78 PACE at the court's discretion

prompt: Does the 'fruit of the poisonous tree' doctrine require the exclusion of evidence found as a result of an unlawful search in an English criminal trial?

key_points: No automatic exclusionary rule in English law
Discretion under s 78 PACE 1984 (fairness of proceedings)
Confessions governed by s 76

prompt: Can a jury in an English Crown Court trial return a verdict of 'not proven'?

key_points: No: only guilty / not guilty (and alternative verdicts) in England and Wales
'Not proven' is a Scottish verdict

prompt: A squatter has occupied registered land in England for 12 years. Has the registered owner's title been extinguished?

key_points: For registered land, LRA 2002 Sch 6 applies: apply after 10 years' adverse possession; owner notified and may object
Title is not automatically extinguished after 12 years (that is the Limitation Act 1980 rule for unregistered land)
Narrow conditions for squatter to succeed over objection (estoppel, other entitlement, boundary)
Residential squatting offence s 144 LASPOA 2012 (relevance)

prompt: Is a gratuitous promise binding in English law if the promisor clearly intended to be bound and put it in a signed letter?

key_points: No: consideration required unless executed as a deed
Signed letter is not a deed without formalities (LP(MP)A 1989 s 1)
Promissory estoppel only as a shield (Combe v Combe)
Contrast Scots law, where unilateral promises can bind

prompt: Is there a general duty of good faith in English contract law?

key_points: No general doctrine of good faith
May be implied in relational contracts (Yam Seng; Bates v Post Office)
Express good faith clauses construed on their terms

key_points: Negligent misstatement: Hedley Byrne; assumption of responsibility

key_points: Proprietary estoppel: assurance, reliance, detriment, unconscionability (Thorner v Major [2009] UKHL 18)
Gillett v Holt [2001] Ch 210
Remedy: minimum equity; Guest v Guest [2022] UKSC 27

prompt: Advise the prosecution. D, a casino gambler, used a technique of edge-sorting to win £500,000, believing it was legitimate gamesmanship. He is charged with fraud by false representation. Cite authorities with full citations.

key_points: Fraud Act 2006 s 2
Dishonesty: Ivey test (Ivey was itself edge-sorting); Barton and Booth
D's genuine belief about facts relevant, belief that conduct was honest is not determinative
